title: Lethal Mutations in the Classroom: When Good Techniques Go Bad
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Continuing her series on 'lethal mutations' in education, Hughes turns from research travelling badly through school systems to how sound techniques can degrade during actual classroom use, even when they arrive intact. She defines a classroom lethal mutation as occurring when 'the visible form of a technique survives, but the learning mechanism that made it useful disappears', and catalogues ten categories including purpose-loss (retrieval becoming disconnected quiz culture), compliance mutations (feedback becoming a marking exchange rather than changed thinking), over-simplification, dependency mutations, premature release, and a newly identified 'conflation mutation' where distinct techniques like think-pair-share and turn-and-talk get blurred together. She closes with four diagnostic questions teachers can ask before using any technique to guard against these mutations.
points: Hughes's core definition - a lethal mutation is when 'the visible form of a technique survives, but the learning mechanism that made it useful disappears' - gives leaders a precise diagnostic lens for observation.
Her example of feedback mutating into a 'marking exchange' (comment, purple-pen response, no behaviour change) exposes how compliance can be mistaken for genuine improvement.
Her newly named 'conflation mutation', where distinct techniques such as think-pair-share and turn-and-talk are blurred together, highlights a subtler failure mode than simple misuse.
She closes with four practical diagnostic questions - what is this for, why now, what could go wrong, how will I know it worked - that teachers can apply before using any technique.
quotes: A classroom lethal mutation happens when the visible form of a technique survives, but the learning mechanism that made it useful disappears.

Retrieval can mutate into quiz culture. Every lesson begins with five questions because that is what we do, but the questions are poorly chosen, disconnected from current learning, too easy, too recent, or never returned to.

In its healthy form, feedback should change future thinking or performance. In mutated form, it becomes a marking exchange: the teacher writes a comment, the pupil responds in purple pen, and the book now contains evidence that feedback occurred.
Cold calling, for example, can be inclusive and powerful. But it mutates when it becomes public exposure. If pupils experience cold calling as a trap, they become anxious, defensive or silent.

Before using a technique, teachers might ask four simple questions. What is this technique for? Why is it useful at this point in the learning? What could go wrong if I use it badly? How will I know whether it has worked?
